name: libplctag
desc: Portable and simple API for accessing AB PLC data over Ethernet
why: A door into Allen-Bradley PLC protocols over Ethernet, letting you talk to real industrial controllers.

brief.what_it_is: libplctag is an open source C library for Linux, Windows and macOS that talks to PLCs over EtherNet/IP or Modbus TCP to read and write tags. Your program passes it a tag name and a PLC address, and it returns the tag's values as integers, floats, bits or arrays of those. The README says it has been in production since early 2012 and supports Rockwell/Allen-Bradley ControlLogix, Micro850, PLC-5, SLC 500 and MicroLogix, plus Omron NX/NJ series. The Homebrew entry lists two executables, modbus_server and tag_rw2, but the README does not describe either one.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a portable, simple API for reading and writing PLC data without tying the user to vendor tooling. It also says the library has very stable API with almost no changes other than feature additions since 2012, and that it is designed for easy wrapping in other languages. The History link points to a wiki page on why it was built, which I did not fetch.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals beyond saying it is a pure C library with no dependencies apart from libc or musl and pthreads on some platforms. It says it uses protocol-specific features for performance and supports multiple requests per packet and packet size negotiation with newer ControlLogix firmware. The API is described as mostly data access, covering single bits and 8 to 64-bit integers and floats.
brief.install_notes: The README does not mention brew. It says to get pre-built ZIP binaries from the GitHub releases page for your system, and it lists 32 and 64-bit builds for x86 Linux and Windows and 64-bit for x86-64 macOS. For a source build it points to a CMake build system and says native CMake support is in recent Visual Studio. Raspberry Pi is supported on Linux and Windows IoT, and the README says some effort is needed to configure Visual Studio for the Windows IoT build. Using it for real work requires a reachable PLC on the network, since the examples read a tag named TestBigArray from a Logix-class Allen-Bradley controller. No PLC is needed to build or run the library itself.
brief.standout: It has been in production for over a decade with an API that has barely changed, and it is the base for several language wrappers, including the popular libplctag.NET, plus Go, Java and Julia. It is dual licensed under MPL 2.0 or LGPL 2+, so it can be embedded in both open and closed projects.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but I could not confirm a date. The README shows CI badges on the release branch and tested toolchains such as GCC 15.2.0, Alpine 3.23 and MSVC 19.44, which suggests recent activity. It has a release badge and a releases page, but I did not see a release date or last commit date on the fetched page.
brief.caveats: The README carries a safety warning: PLCs control equipment, and loss of property, production or life can happen if mistakes are made. The authors say they make no claims about suitability for any purpose. Testing is limited because they do not own all the hardware, and they ask for bug reports from users who have it. Tier One platforms are a fixed list of OS and compiler combinations, and the README notes that Windows IoT needs extra Visual Studio setup. Some features are marked as partial: SLC 500 arrays were not tested, and user-defined structures must be read piece by piece. Wrappers in other languages may carry different licenses. The homepage fetch gave the README only, so I did not check the wiki API page or the examples README.
quotes: libplctag is an open source C library for Linux, Windows and macOS using EtherNet/IP or Modbus TCP to read and write tags in PLCs.
Oh, wait, you want code!   There are many examples in the examples directory.
PLCs control many kinds of equipment and loss of property, production or even life can happen if mistakes in programming or access are made.
Have fun and let us know if this library is useful to you.

entry.title: libplctag
entry.tldr: A small C library that reads and writes tags on Allen-Bradley and Omron PLCs over Ethernet, a way into how industrial controllers talk.
entry.deeper_look:
libplctag is a pure C library that talks to programmable logic controllers over EtherNet/IP or Modbus TCP. You give it a tag name and a PLC address, and it hands back the value as an integer, float, bit, or an array of those. It supports Rockwell/Allen-Bradley ControlLogix, Micro850, PLC-5, SLC 500 and MicroLogix, plus Omron NX/NJ series.

The README frames it as a portable, simple API that avoids tying you to vendor tooling. It has been in production since early 2012, and the README says the API has seen almost no changes other than feature additions since then. It depends on nothing beyond libc (or musl) and pthreads on some platforms, and it is designed to be wrapped. Wrappers exist for .NET (libplctag.NET), Go, Java and Julia.

The idea underneath is that factory-floor equipment exposes its state as named variables on a network. Once you can read a tag, you can log it, graph it, or write it back. The README says it uses protocol-specific features for speed, including multiple requests per packet and packet size negotiation with newer ControlLogix firmware.

The Homebrew formula installs two executables, modbus_server and tag_rw2. The README does not describe either one, so check their `--help` output before assuming what they do.
entry.install:
brew install libplctag
# Talking to a real PLC needs one reachable on your network. Building and running the library itself does not.

entry.whats_unique: It has been in production for over a decade with a very stable API, and it is the base for several language wrappers. It is dual licensed under MPL 2.0 or LGPL 2+, so it can go into both open and closed projects.
entry.caveats: The README warns that PLCs control equipment and mistakes can cause loss of property, production or life, and the authors can't test every hardware model, so real use needs a PLC and care.
